title: Two pointers from both ends
objectives: Solve sorted-array problems with two pointers.

screens.title: Too big
screens.prose: These seven numbers are sorted, smallest first. We want two of them that add to 10. Pointer `i` starts at the left end and `j` at the right end. Their sum is $1 + 15 = 16$, too big.
screens.question: Tap the number whose pointer should move inwards.

hints.text: Moving `i` right swaps 1 for a bigger number. Moving `j` left swaps 15 for a smaller one.
We need a smaller sum.
Moving `j` left replaces 15 with 11, so the sum falls. Tap 15.

feedback.correct: 15 has to go: even with the smallest number, 1, the sum is too big.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The sum is too big. Which move makes it smaller?

byKey.c0: You moved `i` from 1 to 3. The list is sorted, so the sum grows to $3 + 15 = 18$, further from 10.

explain.text: Every number left of 15 is at least 1, so any pair with 15 adds to at least 16. So 15 has no partner that reaches 10, and we drop it for good. `j` moves left to 11.

screens.title: Walk them inwards
screens.prose: Same numbers, same target. Each step, look at the sum. Too big: move `j` left. Too small: move `i` right.
screens.question: Step the pointers until the pair adds to 10.

ops.label: Move `i` right
ops.why: The sum was too big, and moving `i` right made it bigger. Undo and move `j`.

ops.label: Move `i` right
ops.why: 12 is too big, and a bigger left number only adds to it. Undo and move `j`.

ops.label: Move `j` left
ops.why: 9 is too small, and a smaller right number only shrinks it. Undo and move `i`.

ops.label: Move `i` right
ops.why: 11 is too big, and moving `i` right cannot make it smaller. Undo and move `j`.

ops.label: Move `j` left
ops.why: 9 is too small, and moving `j` left cannot make it bigger. Undo and move `i`.

hints.text: Compare each sum with 10 before you choose a move.
16 and 12 are too big, so the first two moves are both `j`.
The moves are: `j`, `j`, `i`, `j`, `i`. The pair is 4 and 6.

feedback.correct: Five moves, and each one dropped a number that could not be in the pair.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Move `j` when the sum is too big and `i` when it is too small.

byKey.m0: You moved `i` while the sum was too big, so it grew to 18.
byKey.m1: You moved `i` while 12 was too big, so it grew to 14.
byKey.m2: You moved `j` while 9 was too small, so it fell to 7.
byKey.m3: You moved `i` while 11 was too big.
byKey.m4: You moved `j` while 9 was too small, so it fell to 7.

explain.text: Each move dropped one number for good: 15, 11, then 1, 8 and 3. The sums were 16, 12, 9, 11, 9 and 10. Checking every pair would have taken up to 21 sums.

screens.title: Pointers that meet
screens.prose: You just ran the **two-pointer** method: one pointer at each end, and each step moves one of them inwards. Now try target 20. No pair adds to 20, so the search runs until `i` and `j` meet.
screens.question: With $n$ numbers and no pair that works, at most how many sums does the method compute?

options.why: That is every pair, the brute force. Each step here drops a number for good, so the steps run out sooner.
That is binary search, which halves the range. Here each step drops only one number.
The loop stops when the pointers meet. The last number left is never added to itself.

hints.text: How many numbers does one step drop?
Count the sums in the caption: there are 7 numbers.
Each sum drops one number, and the loop stops with one number left. That is $n - 1$ sums.

feedback.correct: Six sums for seven numbers, then `i` and `j` meet.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count how many numbers are left after each sum.

explain.text: Each sum drops one number, and the loop stops when one is left. So at most $n - 1$ sums: the method is $O(n)$, against $O(n^2)$ for every pair. `i` and `j` meet on 11 here.

screens.title: Both ends of a word
screens.prose: Two pointers also check a **palindrome**, a word that reads the same both ways. Compare the letters at `i` and `j`. If they match, move both inwards. Stop when the pointers meet.
screens.question: How many comparisons does `refer` need?

widget.accept: 2: r with r, then e with e. The middle f is left alone.
widget.label: Number of comparisons

hints.text: Each comparison checks two letters at once.
After r and e, both pointers land on the f.
r with r, then e with e. Then `i` and `j` meet on f, and the loop stops.

feedback.correct: Two comparisons. The middle letter always matches itself.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each comparison uses one letter from each end.

byKey.middle: You compared the middle f with itself. When `i` and `j` meet, one letter is left, and it always matches.
byKey.every: You counted every letter. Each comparison checks a letter at each end, two at a time.
byKey.four: You counted each pair from both sides. Once r matches r, both pointers move on.

explain.text: r matches r and e matches e, then both pointers sit on f. The loop runs `while i < j`, so it stops there. An even word such as `noon` also takes $4 / 2 = 2$ comparisons.

screens.title: Squares in order
screens.prose: Squaring a sorted list can break its order: $(-7)^2 = 49$ beats $6^2 = 36$. The biggest square is always at one end. So we fill the output from the back, taking the bigger square of the two ends. 49 is placed, and `i` has moved on.
screens.question: Tap the number whose square fills the next slot from the back.

hints.text: Only the two numbers under the pointers can hold the biggest square left.
Square −3 and square 6.
$(-3)^2 = 9$ and $6^2 = 36$. The bigger one, 36, goes next.

feedback.correct: 36 beats 9, so 6 fills the slot and `j` moves left.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the squares of the two numbers under the pointers.

byKey.c1: You took −3, but $(-3)^2 = 9$ is smaller than $6^2 = 36$. Compare squares, not signs.
byKey.c3: 2 is not at an end. Its square, 4, is the second smallest, so it goes in the second slot, not the fifth.
byKey.c2: −1 is nearest zero, so its square, 1, is the smallest of all. It goes first.
byKey.c4: 4 is not at an end. The biggest square left is always under `i` or `j`.

explain.text: 36 goes in the fifth slot and `j` moves to 4. Next, $(-3)^2 = 9$ loses to $4^2 = 16$. One pass gives `[1, 4, 9, 16, 36, 49]`, with no sort.

screens.title: The wrong pointer
screens.prose: Back to target 10. Suppose a walk stands with `i` on 4 and `j` on 8: the sum is 12, too big. A classmate says either pointer can move, since both change the sum. They move `i`.
screens.question: What happens next?

options.text: The search ends with no pair, though $4 + 6 = 10$ exists
It still finds $4 + 6$, one step later
options.why: You assumed a dropped number can come back. Pointers only move inwards, so once `i` leaves 4 the pair is gone.
14 is not the target. The loop stops only on a match or when the pointers meet.
The loop stops when `i` meets `j`, so neither pointer leaves the list.

hints.text: After `i` moves, which numbers can still be paired?
4 is the only partner for 6, and `i` is about to leave it.
Now `i` is on 6: $6 + 8 = 14$, so `j` moves left onto 6. The pointers meet with no pair.

feedback.correct: Moving `i` dropped 4, the only partner for 6.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow the pointers after `i` moves to 6.

byKey.later: You assumed 4 could come back. Each move drops a number for good, so moving the wrong pointer can drop half of the answer.

explain.text: Moving `i` threw away 4, and 4 was half of the answer. Then $6 + 8 = 14$ sends `j` left, and the pointers meet. Moving `j` was safe: 8 plus anything from `i` onwards is at least 12.

canvas.caption: The pointers meet on 6: the pair was skipped

screens.question: Why is the loop condition `i < j` rather than `i <= j`?

options.text: With `i == j` the sum would use one number twice
With `i <= j` the loop would never end
options.why: It would end: one more step makes `i` pass `j`. The problem is that one step adds a number to itself.

options.text: With `i <= j` the pointers would leave the list
options.why: At `i == j` both point at a real number. The loop then adds it to itself, which is not a pair.

feedback.correct: A pair needs two different positions.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. What does `nums[i] + nums[j]` mean when `i == j`?

explain.text: With target 10 and the list `[5]`, `i <= j` would return `(0, 0)`: 5 used twice. `i < j` makes an empty list and a single number return `None` at once.

screens.title: Write both
screens.prose: `two_sum_sorted(nums, target)` returns the indices `(i, j)`, with `i < j`, of two numbers adding to `target`, or `None`. `is_palindrome(s)` compares letters only: skip anything where `str.isalpha()` is false, and ignore case. A string with no letters counts as a palindrome.

state.caption: `'Step on no pets'`: letters only, case ignored

screens.question: Write `two_sum_sorted` and `is_palindrome` with two pointers.

tests.call: is_palindrome('A man, a plan, a canal: Panama')

widget.how: Check runs 15 hidden tests: 7 for `two_sum_sorted` and 8 for `is_palindrome`. One `two_sum_sorted` test has 100,000 numbers, so it must be $O(n)$.

hints.text: Both functions start with `i, j = 0, len(...) - 1` and loop `while i < j`.
In `is_palindrome`, a pointer on a space or a comma moves on without comparing.
If `s[i]` is not a letter, `i += 1`; elif `s[j]` is not, `j -= 1`. Otherwise return `False` if the lower-case letters differ, else move both.

feedback.correct: Both run in one pass with two indices and no copies.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-4: Test 4 is `[5]` with target 10. Returning `(0, 0)` uses 5 twice: loop `while i < j`.
byKey.test-7: Test 7 has 100,000 numbers. Checking every pair is too slow; move one pointer per step.
byKey.test-9: Test 9 has spaces and capitals. Skip non-letters and compare `.lower()` letters.
byKey.test-12: Test 12 is the empty string, which counts as a palindrome. Return `True` when the loop ends.

explain.text: `is_palindrome` moves only one pointer when it meets a non-letter, so `i` and `j` always sit on letters before comparing. Neither function builds a cleaned copy of its input, so the extra space is $O(1)$.

screens.title: Netting two trades
screens.prose: A desk closed seven trades. Their P&Ls in pounds are sorted, worst first. To offset a £50 fee in the report, you need two trades that net exactly £50. Run the two pointers from the ends.
screens.question: Tap the two trades that net £50.

hints.text: The first sum is $-120 + 135 = 15$. Too small, so which pointer moves?
Then $-75 + 135 = 60$ is too big.
15 moves `i`, 60 moves `j`, 15 moves `i` again, then $-40 + 90 = 50$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Step the pointers from the ends and add each pair.

byKey.ends: You took the two ends: $-120 + 135 = 15$, not 50. Move `i` right, since 15 is too small.
byKey.near: $-75 + 135 = 60$ is too big, so `j` moves left. Keep stepping.

explain.text: The sums were 15, 60, 15 and then 50: four steps for seven trades. With 10,000 trades sorted by P&L, the same walk takes at most 9,999 sums, not 50 million.

ideas: On sorted input, a pointer at each end and their sum show which number can never be in the answer. Drop it and move inwards.
Each step drops one number, so the walk is $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ extra space, against $O(n^2)$ for every pair.
The same walk checks palindromes, reverses in place and merges squares of a sorted list from the back.

formula.name: The pointer rule
formula.tex: s < t \Rightarrow i \mathrel{+}= 1, \quad s > t \Rightarrow j \mathrel{-}= 1
formula.note: Loop `while i < j`: a pair needs two different positions.

summary.trap: Moving the wrong pointer drops half of the answer for good, and unsorted input breaks the rule silently.

quiz.prose:
The list is not sorted.

```python
print(two_sum_sorted([8, 3, 5, 1, 9], 10))
```
quiz.question: What does it print?

options.why: That pair, $1 + 9$, does exist. But the pointers never reach it, because the moves assume sorted input.
$8 + 3 = 11$, not 10. The method only returns a pair that hits the target.
The function never checks the order. It runs and quietly gives a wrong answer.

feedback.correct: The moves assume sorted input, so the pair $1 + 9$ is skipped.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Walk the pointers: $8 + 9 = 17$, then $8 + 1 = 9$, and so on.

explain.text: $8 + 9 = 17$ drops 9, the partner of 1, on the first step. The rest of the sums are too small, and the pointers meet. Sort first, in $O(n \log n)$, or use the hash map from two-sum, which needs no order.

quiz.prose:
This loop is meant to reverse a list in place.

```python
xs = [3, 8, 1, 9, 4]
for i in range(len(xs)):
    xs[i], xs[-1 - i] = xs[-1 - i], xs[i]
print(xs)
```
quiz.question: What does it print?

options.why: That is the list after half the loop. The second half swaps every pair back.
Each line swaps two values, so no value is lost or copied.
`xs[-1 - i]` runs from `xs[-1]` to `xs[-5]`, all inside the list.

feedback.correct: Each pair is swapped twice, so the list ends where it began.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. What happens when `i` passes the middle?

explain.text: The loop runs over all five indices. So the pair at 0 and 4 is swapped at `i = 0` and again at `i = 4`. Stop at the middle with `i < j`: `i, j = 0, len(xs) - 1`, swap, then move both inwards.

quiz.prose: A strangle's payoff at six expiry prices, from £90 to £115, is `[10, 5, 0, 0, 5, 10]`. To check it is symmetric, we run the palindrome check on the list.
quiz.question: How many comparisons does the check make?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each comparison uses one value from each end.

byKey.all: You counted every value. Each comparison checks two values at once.
byKey.half: With six values there are three pairs: (0, 5), (1, 4) and (2, 3).

explain.text: An even-length list of 6 has 3 mirror pairs. After the third, `i = 3` and `j = 2`, so `i < j` fails. All three match, so the payoff is symmetric.

options.why: That uses the one 5 twice. `i` and `j` both start at 0, so `while i < j` never runs.
`len(nums) - 1` is 0, a valid index. The loop simply does not run.

feedback.correct: With one number there is no pair, and the loop never starts.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Where do `i` and `j` start for a list of one?

explain.text: `i` and `j` both start at 0, so `i < j` is false at once and the function returns `None`. An empty list gives `j = -1`, which also skips the loop.
